verses.note: The verse puts God before and outside everything that exists. Read as a full sentence, it says the universe has a beginning and that God is its cause; read as a time clause, it still makes God the one who acts on the world. Either way nothing in heaven or earth shares his status.
God names the day and the night. In the ancient world naming expressed authority, so even darkness, which neighboring peoples feared, has its name and place from God.

God does not make a finished, static world but a fruitful one, with seed carrying life forward. Creation has its own God-given capacities, which is why Scripture can praise God both for making the world and for sustaining its seasons.

God's blessing on animals shows that his care reaches beyond humanity. Scripture later has the sea creatures praising God (Psalm 148:7) and Jesus saying that not one sparrow falls apart from the Father (Matthew 10:29).

The whole created order, material and embodied, is very good in God's sight. Paul draws on this when he rejects teachers who forbid marriage and foods, saying everything God created is good (1 Timothy 4:4).

The verse insists that creation was brought to completion. The world as God made it lacked nothing it needed to be good, which is why later disorder in Genesis is presented as damage to a finished work, not as a stage in an unfinished one.

By naming rivers that Israel knew, the text insists that Eden belongs to the same real world as Assyria and the Euphrates. The garden story is not set in a mythic nowhere; it is the beginning of human history on this earth.

The echo of 1:31 shows that corruption is a reversal of creation's goodness, not a flaw in its making. The world God saw as very good is the same world he now sees ruined, and the difference is what creatures did with it.

On the second day God separated the waters above from the waters below; on the third he gathered the seas so that dry land appeared. Verse 11 releases both at once. The flood is creation running backward, and it shows that the world's order holds only because God holds it (Psalm 104:9, Jeremiah 5:22).

The ark is a small creation carried through the collapse of the large one. The same categories God created ‘according to their kinds’ are preserved by kind, so that the world after the flood will be a continuation of the first creation, not a replacement.

The wind over the waters and the drying land that follows repeat the opening of Genesis 1. Judgment has returned the earth almost to the watery state of 1:2, and God begins again from there, which shows that his purpose for creation outlasts his judgment on it.

The blessing that went out to living creatures in Genesis 1 is spoken again over the animals leaving the ark. God's intention for a full and teeming earth was interrupted by judgment but not withdrawn.

Food is still received as God's gift. Paul draws on this pattern when he insists that nothing God created is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:3-5), and the New Testament's declaration that all foods are clean (Mark 7:19) returns to the breadth of this grant.

The blessing names the whole created order, heaven above, the deep below, and the body's power to bear and nurse, and puts all of it in the hand of the God of Jacob. Fertility is God's gift, not the domain of the fertility gods of Canaan.

By echoing Genesis 1:28, the verse presents Israel as the place where God's original blessing on humanity is being carried forward. What God intended for the whole human race takes shape first in one family.

God claims to be the maker of every human body, including bodies that cannot speak, hear, or see. The verse does not explain why people differ in ability, but it refuses to place any person outside God's making and purpose, a point Jesus makes about the man born blind (John 9:1-3).
The world was made with a rhythm of work and rest built in. By keeping the Sabbath, Israel imitates the Creator and confesses that the world and its time belong to him.

Calling unauthorized slaughter bloodshed echoes the covenant with Noah, where God permitted meat but reserved the blood (Genesis 9:3-6). Animal life is given to humanity for use, but it is not humanity's to take as if it were nothing.
Even outside the sanctuary, life belongs to God. Returning the blood to the ground treats the animal's life as something given back, not simply discarded.

The land's fruitfulness is bound up with the people's faithfulness, the pattern of Deuteronomy 28 and of Isaiah's vineyard song. The thorns recall the curse on the ground in Genesis 3:18, and Isaiah's later promises reverse them: instead of the thornbush, the cypress (Isaiah 55:13).

The Creator handles the whole cosmos as a merchant handles grain. The verse does not describe physics; it asserts that nothing in creation is too large for God to have measured, and so nothing in the exiles' world is beyond his reach.

God stretched out the heavens like a tent to live in. The image of creation as a dwelling God pitches for himself runs through the Psalms (104:2) and anticipates the tabernacle, the tent in which God would live among his people.
God's creative work includes the human spirit. The one who formed it is able to renew it, which is exactly what verse 10 promises: a new spirit poured out on the house of David and Jerusalem.
The winds and sea obey Jesus as creatures obey their maker. The verse shows the created order responding to his word as it responded to God's word in Genesis 1.
Jesus makes creation, not later legislation, the measure of marriage. The order God made ‘from the beginning’ still binds, which is why he can use Genesis to judge a practice the law had tolerated.

The sea, which Scripture uses as the image of chaos (Genesis 1:2, Psalm 74:13), obeys Jesus as it obeys its Creator. The verse shows the Creator's authority exercised by a man who a moment before was asleep.

Jesus argues from creation: the God who made both outside and inside claims both. The doctrine of creation undercuts any religion that treats the visible and ritual as God's concern and the inner life as one's own.

Jesus claims that creation itself would acknowledge him if human beings refused. Scripture elsewhere pictures the nonhuman world praising God (Psalm 96:11-13, Psalm 98:8) and groaning for its redemption (Romans 8:19-22); here that witness is focused on the king entering his city.

Everything that exists owes its existence to the Word. That leaves no room for the idea that matter or any power is outside his making, and it grounds John's later claim that the world which rejected him was his own.

Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.15.2) read the mud as the Creator's hand, the same Word who formed Adam from the ground completing what was lacking from birth. The text does not draw the link, but the act of giving sight never had is a work of making, not repair.
The created world is not neutral. By its existence and order it testifies to its Maker, so that the refusal to honor God is a refusal of what creation itself declares (Psalm 19:1-4).
The God of Abraham creates by his word, calling into existence what did not exist. The faith that justifies is faith in the Creator, the reverse of the refusal in 1:20-25 to honor him as Creator.

The world was made good (Genesis 1:31), and its present frustration is not its nature but its condition after the fall. Christian care for creation has often drawn on this passage as evidence that the physical world matters to God's purposes.

The answer rests on the relation between Creator and creature. The creature may cry out, as Job and the psalmists do, but may not stand over God as his judge. Paul's point is not that God is arbitrary but that human beings are not in a position to indict him.

The God who raises the dead is the God who gave each seed its body at creation. Paul grounds resurrection in creation: the power that made bodies in the first place can remake them, and the variety of bodies he already made shows that he is not limited to the present kind.

The Son is creation's origin, agent, and purpose. The verse names both the visible and invisible realms, so nothing in heaven or earth, including angels and spiritual rulers, exists independently of him.
God made the universe through the Son. The Son stands at creation's beginning as agent and at its end as heir, the same pattern as Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3.
Creation is God's handiwork and also temporary: it will grow old and be changed. The Son is its maker and outlasts it, so the believer's hope rests on him rather than on the permanence of the world.
